content.text: A deadlock isn't the database malfunctioning. It's two transactions each holding a lock the other needs, and the engine breaking the cycle by failing one of them. The cycle comes from your code: locks taken in different orders, transactions that stay open, and scans that lock rows you never meant to touch. Design makes deadlocks rare, and a retry of the whole transaction handles the ones that remain.

The order service logs Msg 1205 a few times a week, always at busy hours, and the ticket says "SQL Server deadlock bug under load". Checkout reserves stock and then updates the shipment; the cancellation job updates the shipment and then releases the stock. In a test on SQL Server 2022, two sessions ran those two transactions 300 ms apart, each pausing one second between its two updates. Run three times, it deadlocked three times, with no other load on the server, and the victim was the checkout twice and the cancellation once. With both transactions in the same order, it never deadlocked: the second one simply waited about 0.7 seconds.
The belief: deadlocks are a database malfunction that only happens under extreme load, and application design can't prevent them.

Deadlocks show up at random, mostly in production and mostly when traffic peaks. The error comes from the database and reads as if the engine decided to kill your request. The locks themselves are invisible in ORM code, so nothing in a code review hints at a problem. There's a grain of truth: more traffic means more overlapping transactions, and Microsoft's deadlocks guide says deadlocks can't be completely avoided. But the cycle itself is built by your access pattern, and load only decides how often two requests walk into it.
A deadlock is a cycle, not a slowdown
Blocking ends on its own: the transaction holding the lock finishes and the waiter continues. A

can't end that way, because each transaction waits for the other. SQL Server's lock monitor searches for such cycles every 5 seconds by default, and the interval drops to as low as 100 milliseconds while it keeps finding them. It picks the

, then by which transaction is cheaper to roll back, rolls it back and returns error 1205. In the tests, the cycle was broken about 3.5 and 3.3 seconds after it formed in the first two runs, and about 0.8 seconds in the third, which came right after them. PostgreSQL waits
, one second by default, before checking, and its docs warn that which transaction gets aborted is difficult to predict. The same test on PostgreSQL 18 failed with
line showed the two processes waiting on each other.
Cause 1: the same locks in different orders

The hook is the classic shape. Checkout locks the stock row, then wants the shipment row; cancellation locks the shipment row, then wants the stock row. PostgreSQL's docs name the fix plainly: the best defense is to make sure all applications acquire locks on multiple objects in a consistent order. Pick one order per pair of tables, such as stock before shipments, and update rows within a table in ascending key order. Then the second transaction waits instead of forming a cycle, which is what the same-order runs showed.

Every lock is held until commit, so a longer transaction is a wider target. Microsoft's guide says deadlocks typically occur when several long-running transactions run concurrently, because update and exclusive locks are held longer. In the test, the one-second pause between two updates is what made the overlap certain. In real code, that pause is an HTTP call, a message publish or a user's decision made inside the transaction.
Cause 3: scans lock rows you didn't mean to touch

filtering on a column without an index has to read every row to find its targets, and it locks rows as it checks them. Microsoft's locking guide advises accessing the least amount of data possible in a transaction, which lessens the number of locked rows. In the test, a 1,000-row table had no index on

. Session A updated order 900 and, a second later, order 1; session B updated order 100. Three different rows, yet both runs deadlocked: B's scan stopped at A's row 900, and A's second scan stopped at B's row 100. After adding an index on
, B committed in 4 ms without waiting at all.

hold shared locks to the end, so two transactions that read a row and then update it can deadlock, as the lost updates article showed. Microsoft's deadlocks guide recommends avoiding those levels when they aren't required, and using row versioning, such as
, to minimize deadlocks between reads and writes.

blocks.title: Retry the transaction, not the statement

content.text: After 1205, the whole transaction has already been rolled back. Rerunning only the statement that failed applies half of the work outside any transaction. Replay everything from
, reads included, cap the number of attempts, and log each retry so a rising count gets noticed.
Before changing code, read the deadlock graph. SQL Server's default
session already records every deadlock as an
event, with the statements and the locks involved:

blocks.code:
SELECT x.e.value('@timestamp', 'datetime2') AS [When],
       x.e.query('.') AS Report
FROM (SELECT CAST(t.target_data AS xml) AS data
      FROM sys.dm_xe_session_targets AS t
      JOIN sys.dm_xe_sessions AS s ON s.address = t.event_session_address
      WHERE s.name = N'system_health'
        AND t.target_name = N'ring_buffer') AS rb
CROSS APPLY rb.data.nodes('//event[@name="xml_deadlock_report"]') AS x(e);

blocks.title: PostgreSQL keeps the details in the server log

content.text: The client only sees process IDs; in the test, the error's hint said to see the server log for query details. Also turn on
, which is off by default: every lock wait longer than
is then logged, near misses included.
How to apply it in your project
Run the query above, or check the PostgreSQL server log, and group deadlocks by the pair of statements involved.

For each pair of tables updated together, choose one order and use it everywhere; within a table, update rows by ascending key. Shared data-access code or stored procedures make the order hard to break.

Two sessions were enough: opposite update orders deadlocked in every test run, and the same order never did.
Long transactions and scans caused by missing indexes widen the window; an index removed a deadlock between three different rows.
when not needed, and use row versioning for reads.
Deadlocks can't be eliminated, so retry the whole transaction with a short random pause and watch how often it happens.
